title: The Men Who Opened the Book
subtitle: A doctor, a squire, some clerks and a showman
blurb: The list of demons was handed down by a sceptic, a mocker, a chain of nameless copyists and Aleister Crowley, and hardly one of them believed in it the way you would expect.

segments.t: Fifteen sixty-three. A town on the lower Rhine. A physician sits down at his desk to write the most dangerous kind of book there is. Not a book of spells. Those are common. This one says the witches are innocent.

Last night we watched old gods get demoted into demons. Tonight, the people. Because somebody had to write the seventy-two names down, and copy them, and print them. And here is the strange part. Almost none of them believed in the book the way you would expect.

His name is Johann Weyer. As a boy he studied under the most notorious magician in Europe, Cornelius Agrippa, and came away with one firm lesson. People swore that Agrippa's black dog was a demon. Weyer had walked it on a lead. It was a dog. He grows up to be court physician to the Duke of Cleves, and he never forgets that dog.

His book is called On the Illusions of Demons, and its argument is outrageous for its day. The women being burned across Europe are not sorceresses. They are old, or ill, or deluded, or they were tortured until they said whatever would make it stop. I should be honest. Weyer believes in the Devil. He simply thinks the Devil's best trick is fooling the judges. Treat these women, he says. Do not kill them.

Then, in fifteen seventy-seven, he adds an appendix. He has got hold of an older manuscript, a catalogue he calls the book of the offices of spirits. An office here means a job. Sixty-nine demons, with their ranks, their shapes and their legions. Where it came from, nobody knows. The manuscript itself is lost.

He prints it as an exhibit. Look, he is saying, at what the conjurors actually believe. And he gives it a title that is a sneer. Pseudomonarchia Daemonum. The false monarchy of demons. He is careful, too. He tells his reader that he has cut passages out on purpose, the working parts, so that no curious fool can try it. A list of names with the engine removed. Hold on to that. It is the first joke of the night, and it takes a century to land.

Here is one of the sixty-nine, and I choose him because a physician might have liked him. Bathin. A duke, mighty and strong, with thirty legions. He appears as a strong man with the tail of a serpent, sitting on a pale horse.
He knoweth the Virtues of Herbs and Precious Stones, and can transport men suddenly from one country to another.

Herbs and stones. That is an apothecary on a horse. His seal is in your grimoire now. And notice the second gift, sudden transport from one country to another. Because that is exactly what is about to happen to the list.

threshold.q: Before we cross the water. You are Weyer. You are holding a manuscript of sixty-nine demons, and you think it is poison. What do you do with it?

opts.label: Print it, teeth pulled
opts.reply: Then you are Weyer to the letter. Show the evidence, remove the danger, trust the reader. It is the decent, scholarly thing to do. It is also how the list reached every person who came after him. Good intentions are excellent carriers. Watch what happens to yours.

opts.label: Burn it
opts.reply: Clean. Final. And I think you would have hesitated with the candle in your hand, the way everyone does. Somebody burned Weyer's source, or lost it, and here we are regardless, because he had already copied it. Burning only works if you are first. Nobody is ever first.

opts.label: Keep it in a drawer
opts.reply: The honest answer. Not published, not destroyed, just kept, for nights when the house is quiet. That is how most of these manuscripts actually survived. Not in libraries. In drawers, belonging to people who would have told you they did not believe a word.

segments.t: Kent, in the south of England. Fifteen eighty-four. A country gentleman named Reginald Scot, whose only other book is about growing hops, is angry. He has watched witch trials in his own county and he thinks them a disgrace. So he writes The Discoverie of Witchcraft. Discoverie in the old sense. Uncovering. Exposure.
Scot has read Weyer, and he lifts the whole list into English, so that plain readers can laugh at it. Here is one entry as he printed it. Listen to the bird.

Halphas is a great earl, and cometh abroad like a stork, with a hoarse voice, he notably buildeth up towns full of munition and weapons, he sendeth men of war to places appointed, and hath under him six and twenty legions.
segments.src: Scot, The Discoverie of Witchcraft (1584), book 15, spelling modernised

segments.t: A stork. Remember the stork. Now, tradition says that when King James came to the English throne he had every copy of Scot's book burned. It is a fine story, and historians doubt it. No record of any burning has been found. What is documented is that James loathed the book, and said so in print, in his own treatise on demons, where he calls Scot's opinions damnable.

And here is the second joke. To mock the conjurors, Scot printed their material in plain English, in a book anyone could buy. So for the next hundred years, if you were an English village magician who wanted to raise a spirit, the handiest manual on the market was the book written to stop you. The debunking became the handbook.

Now the sixteen hundreds, and people with no names at all. Scribes. Clerks. Somebody takes the list, most likely from Scot's English, and starts improving it. They shuffle the order. They draw a seal for every spirit. They lose one, called Pruflas, who had already slipped out of Scot's translation by accident. And they add four that Weyer never had. Vassago, Seere, Dantalion, Andromalius. Sixty-nine becomes seventy-two.

They are, if you will forgive me, fan editors. They have a text they love and they cannot leave it alone. One elaborate copy carries the name of a Doctor Thomas Rudd, and gives every demon an angel to hold its leash. Whether Rudd himself ever touched it is doubted. The copy we have was written out long after his death. But notice what all of them have done. They have put the engine back.

And things drift, the way they do in copying. Remember the stork? In the finished book he is still Halphas, an earl with twenty-six legions, but now he comes as a stock-dove. A wood pigeon. Nobody knows which pen changed the bird. He still speaks with a hoarse voice. And Scot's towns have become towers. He builds them, furnishes them with ammunition and weapons, and sends men-of-war to places appointed. A pigeon who is an arms contractor.

His neighbour on the page is the other builder. Malphas. A president, mighty and powerful, with forty legions. He arrives as a crow, and will put on human shape if the conjuror asks, and he too is hoarse. He builds houses and high towers. He tells you what your enemies desire, and think, and have done. He gives good familiars, meaning helpful attendant spirits. And then the book adds a warning.
If thou makest a Sacrifice unto him he will receive it kindly and willingly, but he will deceive him that doth it.

Receives it kindly, and then deceives. I think of Malphas as the patron of this whole enterprise. Weyer offered the list his contempt. Scot offered it his mockery. The list accepted both, very graciously, and then did exactly as it pleased.

threshold.q: So pick a side. The doctor, who pulled the teeth out of the book to save lives? Or the nameless copyists, who lovingly put every tooth back?

opts.label: The doctor
opts.reply: A good side to be on. Weyer's book did real work. Historians still argue over how many lives it touched, but it gave doubt a respectable voice. And yet without the appendix he was faintly ashamed of, you and I would have nothing to talk about tonight. He would hate that. I rather enjoy it.

opts.label: The copyists
opts.reply: Of course. They are the ones who loved it. A list of names is only evidence. A list with seals, and circles, and a king with a ring behind it, is a world. They were not being careful. They were being generous. Most of what haunts you in this book is their handwriting.

opts.label: Whoever kept the drafts
opts.reply: The archivist's answer, and the hardest side to join, because almost nobody did keep them. Weyer's source is gone. The first Goetia is gone. What we have are copies of copies, arguing with each other in brown ink. If you enjoy that argument, you are already one of the clerks.

segments.t: Two hundred years go by. The manuscripts wash up where everything washes up, in the British Museum. And in the eighteen eighties a lean, fierce, permanently penniless man sits in its round reading room, copying them out by hand. Samuel Liddell Mathers. He adds MacGregor to his name, for the sake of a Highland ancestry he was very sure of and nobody else was.

In eighteen eighty-eight Mathers helps to found the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn. A secret society for ceremonial magic, in London, with robes, grades and written examinations. Its members include the poet Yeats. And in eighteen ninety-eight it admits a young man with a Cambridge education, a fortune inherited from the family brewery, and no brakes whatever. Aleister Crowley. Mountaineer, chess player, poet of very uneven quality. Mathers thinks him brilliant. Most of the Order cannot stand him.

Crowley buys a house called Boleskine, above Loch Ness, and begins styling himself its laird. In nineteen hundred the London members revolt against Mathers, and Crowley is sent to seize the Order's rooms. By the usual account he arrives in Highland dress and a black mask. The members fetch a constable. That is the great magical war of London. It ends with a policeman on the stairs.

Then master and pupil quarrel too. And in nineteen oh four, from Boleskine, Crowley publishes Mathers's transcript of the Goetia. The very text the other voice has been reading to you all these nights. Mathers's name is not on the title page. It says the book was translated by a dead hand. Mathers was alive. A note explains that the translator had unhappily succumbed to the assaults of four great princes of the spirits. It may be the rudest preface ever printed.

If Crowley has a spirit in this book, it is the twenty-third. Aim. A great strong duke with twenty-six legions. A very handsome man, the book says, but with three heads. The first a serpent's. The second a man's, with two stars on his forehead. The third a calf's, which in Weyer and Scot was a cat's. The copyists again.
He rideth on a Viper, carrying a Firebrand in his Hand, wherewith he setteth cities, castles, and great Places, on fire.

And when he is not burning cities, Aim makes you witty in all manner of ways, and gives true answers about private matters. Set fire to the place and be amusing about it. That is very nearly Crowley's whole career.

Then Crowley does the strangest thing of all. He opens the book with an essay of his own. And in it the wickedest man in England, as the newspapers would later call him, calmly explains that there are no demons.
The spirits of the Goetia are portions of the human brain.
segments.src: Crowley, The Initiated Interpretation of Ceremonial Magic, in Goetia (1904)

segments.t: Portions of the human brain. The seals, he says, are ways of stirring those portions through the eye. Whether he believed it for long is another matter. Crowley believed a great many things, often before breakfast. But the idea outlived him, and tomorrow it gets the whole night.

So count them up. A doctor who printed the list to prove it false. A squire who translated it to laugh at it. Clerks who tinkered with it like a hobby. A showman who took it and then explained it away. Hardly a simple believer in the chain. This book did not survive on faith. It survived because nobody, however sensible, could quite bring himself to throw it away. It is too interesting. You are on your tenth night. You know.

Tomorrow, The Demon in the Mirror. If the spirits are portions of the brain, then whose brain? We follow the seventy-two into psychology, into films and games, and we ask the sceptic's question fairly. Why does this still pull?

Until then. Close the cover gently. Cleverer people than us have failed to keep it shut. And if a crow lands on your windowsill tonight and offers to build you a house, be civil. Just do not give him anything.

glossary.term: Book of the Offices of Spirits
glossary.def: The older manuscript catalogue of demons that Johann Weyer says he copied. It is lost; an office here means a spirit's job or function.
The False Monarchy of Demons. A list of sixty-nine spirits that the physician Johann Weyer added to his book against witch-hunting in 1577. The main ancestor of the Goetia.
Reginald Scot's sceptical book of 1584, which put Weyer's list of demons into English in order to mock it, and was then used as a source by magicians.

glossary.term: Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn
glossary.def: A London society for ceremonial magic founded in 1888 by William Wynn Westcott, Samuel Liddell MacGregor Mathers and William Robert Woodman. Yeats and Crowley were both members.
Aleister Crowley's short essay at the front of the 1904 Goetia, which argues that the spirits are parts of the human brain and the ritual a way of stimulating them.
